primer.intro: A sliding window turns a nested-loops question - the best contiguous stretch satisfying some condition - into a single pass. Two indices mark the window's ends. The right end eats one new element per step; whenever the window breaks its rule, the left end walks forward just far enough to mend it. Nothing is ever re-scanned, because both ends only move forward. The craft lies in naming the rule before coding: at most k zeros inside, at most two distinct fruits, all characters unique. State the invariant in one sentence, and the loop writes itself; skip that sentence, and every off-by-one in the topic finds you.
whenToUse: Longest or shortest contiguous stretch under a budget: distinct letters, zeros to flip, edits allowed.
The rule is monotone - growing the window can only break it, shrinking can only mend it.
Counting substrings with at most k of something; exactly k is then a subtraction of two such counts.
A fixed take from the two ends - the complement is a fixed-length window in the middle.
A frequency table plus two indices can replace re-scanning every substring.
primer.mentalModel: Picture a caterpillar on the array: the head creeps forward one cell per step, and when the body grows too long for the rule, the tail catches up. The window's memory is a small table - counts per letter, a zero counter - fed on entry and drained on exit. Two facts carry every proof in this topic. First, distinct falls only when a count reaches exactly zero, which is why shrinking is a while loop, since evicting one cell may free nothing. Second, each pointer moves at most n steps in the whole run, so the total work is linear no matter how uneven single steps look. Update the answer only while the rule holds - a measurement taken mid-repair measures a broken window.
mistakes: Shrinking with an if instead of a while - one eviction may fail to restore the rule.
Updating the best answer while the window is still invalid, mid-repair.
Moving the left pointer while forgetting the exit bookkeeping - the table keeps counts for cells already gone.

example.title: Longest substring with all characters distinct
example.explain: The map remembers each character's most recent position. When the new character already occurs inside the window, the left end teleports to one past that earlier copy - a shortcut for the usual while loop of evictions. Taking the larger of the old and new left keeps the pointer from ever sliding backward. Both ends move at most n steps, so the pass is linear, and the best length is read off after every single step because this window is always valid.

primer.practice: Open Practice with Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters; every later problem swaps in a new invariant but keeps this exact loop.

sections.title: Grow right, shrink left
sections.text: The loop skeleton is always the same four lines. Add the right element to the window's table. While the rule is broken, remove the left element from the table and advance left. If the rule holds, offer the current width as a candidate answer. The only part that changes between problems is the rule and its table: a zero counter for flip budgets, a distinct counter for fruit types, count minus max frequency for replacements. Write the rule as a boolean over the table before touching the loop, then let the skeleton do what it always does.

check.prompt: A window tracking at most k distinct letters just grew and now holds k+1 kinds. What restores the rule?

options.text: Advance left repeatedly until some letter's count drops to exactly zero
options.explain: Only a count hitting zero reduces the number of kinds inside.

options.text: Advance left exactly one step
options.explain: The departing letter may still occur further inside - the kinds count would stay k+1.

options.text: Jump left all the way to right
options.explain: That discards every candidate stretch in between unexamined.

options.text: Move the right end back one step
options.explain: The right end only advances; retreating would re-scan and break linearity.

reveal.solution: Evicting one cell only decrements a count; the letter may survive elsewhere in the window, leaving k+1 kinds intact. So the shrink is a while loop: remove the left letter from the table, advance left, and stop at the first moment a count reaches zero - that is when a kind truly leaves the window and the rule is whole again.

sections.title: Budgets and complements
sections.text: Two reframings unlock most of the harder problems. The budget: flipping at most k zeros means keeping a window whose zero-count stays at most k - nothing is actually flipped. Replacing at most k letters means window length minus the top letter frequency stays at most k - the deficit is the repair bill. The complement: taking exactly k cards from the two ends leaves a contiguous middle window of fixed length n minus k, so maximising the take is minimising that middle - slide a fixed-width window once and keep its smallest sum. And counting stretches with exactly k kinds is the count with at most k minus the count with at most k minus 1.

quiz.prompt: Longest run of 1s after flipping at most k 0s. Which reframing fits?

options.text: Longest window containing at most k zeros - flip nothing, just tolerate
options.explain: Inside such a window the k flips would finish the job; the widest one is the answer.

options.text: Flip the first k zeros, then measure
options.explain: The best zeros to spend on may sit anywhere, so committing early loses.

options.text: Try every pair of endpoints
options.explain: Quadratic pairs, and the budget check per pair adds more.

options.text: Count the total number of 1s
options.explain: The run must be contiguous; a global count ignores position entirely.

quiz.prompt: Two baskets, each holding one fruit type; pick a contiguous stretch of trees. The window rule?

options.text: At most two distinct values inside the window
options.explain: Baskets are types: the stretch is pickable exactly when it has two kinds or fewer.

options.text: At most two of each fruit
options.explain: Quantity is unlimited - the baskets constrain kinds, numbers are free.

options.text: Exactly two distinct values, no fewer
options.explain: A single-type stretch is also pickable and can be the longest.

options.text: The two most frequent fruits overall
options.explain: Global frequency says nothing about one contiguous stretch.

quiz.prompt: Take exactly k cards from the two ends of a row to maximise their sum. The linear trick?

options.text: Minimise the fixed-length middle window of n-k cards the take leaves behind
options.explain: Ends taken and middle left are complements; best take equals total minus smallest middle.

options.text: Always take the larger end card
options.explain: Greedy commits one card at a time and misses splits that pay off later.

options.text: Take all k from whichever end sums higher
options.explain: The optimum may split between the ends in any proportion.

options.text: Sort the cards and take the k largest
options.explain: Only end cards are reachable; sorting invents picks that are illegal.

quiz.prompt: Count subarrays with exactly k distinct values, given a routine for the at-most version. How?

options.text: atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1)
options.explain: Every exactly-k subarray is in the first count and absent from the second.

options.text: atMost(k) divided by k
options.explain: The counts share no such ratio; the subtraction is exact, division is folklore.

options.text: Run atMost(k) and filter afterwards
options.explain: atMost returns a number, so there is nothing left to filter.

options.text: atMost(k+1) minus atMost(k)
options.explain: That counts subarrays with exactly k+1 kinds, one off.

quiz.prompt: Longest substring with all distinct characters in pwwkew?

options.explain: wke (and kew) has three distinct letters; any longer stretch repeats a w.
pw starts things, but wke beats it after the window jumps past the repeat.
wwkew holds two w's - the window may only hold one of each.
The whole string repeats w twice over.

quiz.prompt: Bits 1 0 1 0 1 with k = 1 flip. What is the longest run of 1s achievable?

options.explain: Flip either zero: 1 0 1 around it becomes 1 1 1. Both zeros in one window needs k = 2.
The whole row holds two zeros, one over the budget.
Even with no flips a 1 plus a flipped neighbour gives 2; one flip does better.
Any four consecutive cells here contain both zeros.

quiz.prompt: Fruit types along the row: 1 2 3 2 2. Longest stretch pickable with two baskets?

options.explain: 2 3 2 2 uses kinds 2 and 3 only; adding the leading 1 makes a third kind.
3 2 2 works, but one more tree to the left still fits the two kinds.
The full row has kinds 1, 2 and 3 - one basket short.
Windows well beyond length 2 satisfy the two-kind rule here.

quiz.prompt: Why is the grow-shrink window linear despite its nested-looking loops?

options.text: Each pointer only advances, so together they take at most 2n steps
options.explain: The inner while spends left-steps, and left has only n to spend in the whole run.

options.text: The inner loop runs at most once per outer step
options.explain: Single steps can shrink many times; it is the total that is bounded, per pointer.

options.text: The table lookups are logarithmic
options.explain: Table updates are constant; the argument is about pointer movement.

options.text: It is quadratic, but fast in practice
options.explain: The bound is genuinely linear - charge each shrink to the cell evicted.

quiz.prompt: Longest repeating-character replacement with a 26-letter count table: total cost?

options.text: Linear in n, with constant-time table updates per step
options.explain: One letter enters, at most one leaves, per step; 26 is a constant lid.

options.text: Quadratic - every window is re-counted
options.explain: The table carries counts across steps precisely so nothing is re-counted.

options.text: n times 2 to the 26
options.explain: Subsets of the alphabet play no role; only counts do.

options.text: n log n
options.explain: Nothing is sorted or searched; both pointers just walk forward.

quiz.prompt: This window sometimes reports stretches holding more than k kinds. Why?

options.text: One eviction may leave distinct above k when the evicted letter repeats inside - use while
options.explain: The if mends nothing unless a count hits zero; best then measures a broken window.

options.text: best must be updated before the if
options.explain: Even earlier measurement would include the just-broken window more often.

options.text: l must start at 1
options.explain: Zero-based l is right; the repair loop is what falls short.

options.text: add must come after the if
options.explain: Adding first is the standard order; the rule check must just be a loop.

quiz.prompt: This shrink loop hangs forever on some inputs. Why?

options.text: l moves but zeros is unchanged - decrement it when the departing bit is 0
options.explain: Without exit bookkeeping the condition can stay true while l runs off the array.

options.text: The guard should be zeros >= k
options.explain: At exactly k the window is legal; the guard is right, the body is empty of bookkeeping.

options.text: r should advance here instead
options.explain: Growing is the outer loop's job; shrinking must fix the budget.

options.text: zeros was initialised too high
options.explain: Any start value still requires the body to change it; the loop body is the fault.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for the k-flips longest-ones window?

options.text: k at least the total number of zeros
options.explain: The window must swallow the whole array and return n - shrink logic must idle cleanly.

options.text: An array of all ones with k = 1
options.explain: Covered by the same code path as any zero-free prefix.

options.text: Strictly alternating bits
options.explain: A pretty pattern, but no special branch fires on it.

options.text: A single-element array
options.explain: Worth a test eventually, yet the swallow-everything case breaks real code more often.
